+"""Render a LinkedIn-ready summary of verified Atira run results."""
+
+from __future__ import annotations
+
+from pathlib import Path
+
+import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
+from matplotlib.patches import FancyBboxPatch
+
+
+OUT = Path(__file__).with_name("atira-run-evolution.png")
+
+
+def minutes(seconds: int) -> str:
+    return f"{seconds // 60}:{seconds % 60:02d}"
+
+
+def rounded_panel(ax, x: float, y: float, width: float, height: float, color: str) -> None:
+    ax.add_patch(
+        FancyBboxPatch(
+            (x, y), width, height,
+            boxstyle="round,pad=0.012,rounding_size=0.025",
+            linewidth=0,
+            facecolor=color,
+            transform=ax.transAxes,
+        )
+    )
+
+

+    # Verified, high-level run facts only. No scenario answers are embedded.

+    left.set_axisbelow(True)
+    left.set_title("QUALITY BREAKTHROUGH", loc="left", color=pale,

Copy-ready post:

We tried. We failed. We tried again—and failed better.

The final hours changed everything.

At the TUM.ai EHL Grand Finale, our first public test scored 10/100 and took 12:19. We kept iterating until we reached a fully eligible 100/100 public run in 5:10.

Then we focused on speed and repeatability. Our final three private-dataset runs were all eligible, achieved the same 66.3 quality score, and completed in 2:05, 1:43, and 2:45. Our fastest valid private run was 86% faster than where we started.

What made the system robust:

- LLM-directed browsing instead of hard-coded website flows
- Evidence-first extraction, source tracking, and coverage checks
- Exact Decimal-based commercial calculations
- Four parallel browsers, action verification, recovery paths, and pre-submit review gates

The honest lesson: correctness and speed are separate challenges. First, we proved the agent could solve the full task correctly. Then we made it much faster and repeatable under pressure.

I exhausted my weekly Claude and Gemini limits and burned roughly $220 in OpenAI credits—but I learned more about agentic AI, reliability engineering, and building under pressure than I could have imagined. It was one of the best weekends of my life.

We tried. We failed. We tried again—but every time, we failed better.

The final hours changed everything.

At the TUM.ai EHL Grand Finale, I built an agentic RFQ-to-Bid system that could navigate unfamiliar enterprise websites, find the right documents, extract evidence, calculate a commercial bid, and submit it end to end.

What made it robust:

- LLM-directed browsing instead of hard-coded website flows
- Evidence-first extraction, source tracking, and coverage checks
- Exact Decimal-based commercial calculations
- Four parallel browsers, action verification, recovery paths, and pre-submit review gates

The biggest lesson: correctness and speed are separate challenges. Building reliable agents is not about one perfect prompt—it is about validation, recovery, structured evidence, and relentless iteration.

I exhausted my weekly Claude and Gemini limits, burned roughly $220 in OpenAI credits, and ran on almost no sleep. But I learned more about agentic AI, reliability engineering, and building under pressure than I could have imagined.

It was one of the best weekends of my life.
